runs.text: outros trabalhadores fora do jantar, ou comer

lines.note: The opening continues an entry from the preceding page: other workers receive something outside the regular dinner or meal. Jantar and comer belong to the Portuguese explanation, not to a new entry.
Ordinario completes comer ordinario, the ordinary meal. This short continuation is a separate physical body row.
Kyou denotes pleasure or entertaining charm here; qiô is an alternative spelling introduced by Latin l. Both long-o marks are circumflexes, and Vt introduces the examples below.
Kyou wo moyousu means arousing pleasure or interest. The Portuguese translation divides prazer after pra-; the Japanese object particle remains attached as printed.

Prazer ends at the beginning of this row. Kangen no kyou ni jouzuru describes becoming absorbed in the pleasure of instrumental music; the tilde in Quanguẽ abbreviates nasal material and is not a long-vowel accent.

runs.text: leuarſe no gosto, & graça da muſica. ¶

lines.note: En-levarse completes the translation as being carried away by the enjoyment and charm of music. The next Japanese example begins Qeô and continues with its object particle on the following row.
Qeô uo samasu means cooling or spoiling enjoyment. The initial uo belongs to the preceding row's noun, not to an independent word or entry.
Kyou samegao ni naru describes taking on a visibly disappointed or disenchanted expression. Fazer-se and tornar-se, divided between rows, are alternative Portuguese renderings.

runs.text: tornarſe no exterior enxabido, desgostoſo; ou eſ-

lines.note: The gloss specifies an outwardly flat, displeased, or startled appearance. The final eſ- continues into espantado below; the historical enxabido is retained.
Espantado completes the preceding description. Kyougatta koto wo yuu means saying eccentric or extravagant things; the Portuguese verb dizer is divided after Di-.
The translation completes 'say extravagant things'. Qeôgarimo- begins kyougarimono, a person characterized by such eccentricity, rather than a Portuguese continuation.
No completes kyougarimono; kyougatta hito supplies an alternative expression. The Portuguese singular means an unusual or eccentric person here, not numerically a single man.
Extrauagante completes the description of the eccentric person. It closes the pleasure/eccentricity entry before the separate homograph meaning today.
This independent kyou/qiou entry means today. Oje is the printed historical Portuguese form; it is not silently changed to hoje.
Kyouaku is explained by warushi and aku. The Portuguese distinguishes evils of fault from evils of punishment, whose second member continues below.
Depena completes the contrast between culpa and pena. The visibly close-set depena is retained rather than normalized to de pena.
Kyouhou is explained as oshiyuru nori, a teaching or doctrine. The scan supports Qeôbô, correcting the OCR's spurious internal space and c for e.
The relative clause completes the definition: a law or doctrine that teaches outwardly. Exterior is retained without replacing the dictionary's formulation with a modern doctrinal interpretation.

Majiuari and cuuauaru explain joining or mixing, matching Miſtura. The final upright S is a written-usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese noun. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Kyoukai is explained by oshie and imashime, instruction and admonition. Dou- begins doutrina, whose preceptive sense is developed in the following two rows.

runs.text: trina, em que ſe manda, ou prohibe algũa cou-

lines.note: The doctrine commands or forbids something. The abbreviation tilde is over u in algũa, and cou- continues the noun cousa below.
Completes cousa por preceito: something required or prohibited by precept. The row is a genuine continuation, not furniture.

The headword denotes the railings or balusters of a bridge. The scan has no secure long-o mark in Qeocan, so the unaccented form is retained rather than regularized from neighboring Qeô entries. The supplied NINJAL lexical index corroborates this form but does not determine its typography (Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, v202510; NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima, Taichi Aida; CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html).
Kyouchuu is explained literally as mune no uchi, inside the breast. The gloss then extends to the interior or mind; the headword's u carries a caron.
The example contrasts a broad interior or mind with a narrow one below. The scan reads Qeôchǔga, without the OCR's extra i after Q; firoi means broad.

runs.text: er muito ſaber, ou pouco, ou pou-

lines.note: Xebai supplies the narrow alternative. The dictionary interprets breadth of mind as possessing much learning, or little learning in the contrasting case; pou- begins poucas.
Completes poucas letras e artes: little literary learning and skill. This continues the knowledge metaphor, rather than introducing a bodily measurement.
Yuku sue identifies the future or what lies ahead, matching daqui por diante. The two o marks in Qeǒcô differ: caron first, circumflex second.
Completes the alternative Portuguese phrase a o diante. The physical break between a and o is retained without combining the words across rows.

runs.text: Em breue eſpaço. Eſte he o ſentido

lines.note: The first gloss gives a short interval. The following qualification contrasts current usage with what the compilers regard as the word's original sense.

runs.text: mais corrente desta palaura, posto que o proprio

lines.note: This is described as the more current sense of the word, although its proper or original meaning is different. The scan's st forms are retained without a global long-s substitution.

runs.text: & originalhe, Agora ha pouco, ou neſte tẽpo

lines.note: The original meaning is said to be just now, a little while ago, or at this present time. Originalhe retains the printed close setting, and tẽpo retains the abbreviation tilde.
Dagora completes neste tempo dagora, this present time. It closes the temporal explanation before the next headword.
Kyoukotsu denotes something inappropriate or absurd in this gloss. Reinspection supports deſconueniente, with e rather than OCR a; the next row completes fora de proposito.
The Portuguese compares it to nonsense or an absurdity. Qeǒcot- begins the adjectival example continued below; the OCR's internal space after Q is not supported.
Qeǒcot-na koto wo yuu means saying inappropriate or absurd things. The line ends inside Portuguese desbarates, not inside the Japanese example.

runs.text: tes, & fora de propoſito. ¶ Item, Couſa

lines.note: Desbarates and fora de proposito complete the first sense. Item then introduces something said lightly or without due consideration.

runs.text: que hum diz leuemente, & com pouca conſi-

lines.note: The second sense concerns speaking lightly and with little consideration. Hum is the historical indefinite pronoun, and conſi- continues below.
Deração completes consideração, closing the thoughtlessness gloss. The cedilla and nasal ending are visible in this short continuation.
Kyoukun, shinan, and kyouke are grouped as counsel or instruction. The two l markers introduce alternatives, not Japanese syllables.
Advice and doctrine complete the counsel gloss. These Portuguese alternatives belong to all three preceding Japanese expressions.
The dictionary itself prefers Qeôto to Qeôdo, as indicated by italic Meliùs. Warui tomogara explains bad associates; both printed headword forms must therefore be retained.
Itazuramono supplies another description of an idle or dissolute person. The visible double z is retained, and the Portuguese adjective phrase continues below.
Maos custumes completes the description as a person of bad habits. Neither the unaccented maos nor the historical custumes is modernized.
Uyamai and ogamu explain reverence and worship. The initial v letters are historical spellings, and reuerẽ- carries a nasal abbreviation before the line break.
Completes reverencia and adds adoration. The final S is the written-usage label, separated typographically from the Portuguese gloss.
Akatsuki no kaze identifies a dawn wind. The visible mark over u is a caron, giving Qeôfǔ rather than OCR Qeôfù; ma- continues into the formerly misclassified body row below.

Drugada completes madrugada, the dawn in the preceding wind definition. This is body text, not bottom furniture; the scan also supplies the omitted final S usage label. The original ID is retained when the row is moved into Column 1.
The Japanese explanation describes comparing and matching, agreeing with cotejar. The line ends in cou, with neither the OCR's extra l nor a secure hyphen; the next row completes cousa.

runs.text: ſa com outra, ou ver ſe està errada, &c.

lines.note: Completes comparing one thing with another, or checking whether it is wrong. Està retains its printed grave accent.
Soragoto explains a falsehood or lie. The headword Qeogon is unaccented in this impression; an expected long-vowel mark is not supplied.
The example means saying a falsehood or making a false allegation. The visible repeated word is Qeogonuo, correcting OCR Q cogonuo without adding an accent.
Completes the translation as raising false testimony. Aleuantar preserves the historical u/v spelling, and the allegation sense explains iy caquru above.
The entry concerns doctrine or commentary on a sacred text. The scan supports guiô, not OCR gurô, with a circumflex on the final o; the following entry has a different final mark.

The explanation identifies the text as the book of Shaka. Xaca is a whole Japanese name embedded in Portuguese. Focused typeface reinspection confirms that it shares the surrounding italic font; the capital X alone is not evidence for roman type.
This distinct entry is simply glossed as books. Its final o has a caron, unlike the circumflex in Qeǒguiô above; the two entries must not be merged.
Oshie no kokoro is the meaning or purport of a teaching. The headword's internal hyphen distinguishes its vowel sequence and is not a line-break mark.
Completes sentido dalguma doutrina, the meaning of a doctrine. Both the nasal abbreviation across the break and the u-carried tilde in dalgũa are retained.
Ashii koto identifies something bad, such as hardship or trouble. This noun entry is distinct from the pleasure verb that follows two rows later.
Evils or misfortunes complete the examples of a bad occurrence. The short row closes this sense before the following verb paradigm.
Kyouji, kyouzuru, kyoujita expresses enjoyment. The Portuguese reads deuer, 'to see' after folgar, rather than the OCR's deuir; the historical close setting and u for v are retained.

The gloss adds taking pleasure in something. Core- begins the quotation's kore, divided from its following object particle by the physical row break; the terminal mark is a hyphen rather than the OCR period.

runs.text: uo qeôjita fitono coixiſani tçuqixenu mo

lines.note: The quotation describes longing for the person who enjoyed this, with tears that never run out. Despite abrasion in the middle of coixiſani, the surviving strokes and the coherent construction support qeôjita and coixiſani, correcting the OCR accent and extra r; the latter is koishisa ni, not a malformed coixisanri. Mo continues into mono below without a visible hyphen.
Mono wa namida nari completes the statement that the inexhaustible thing is tears. Upright Feiq. is the citation label; italic Lib. 1 and Cõ begin the reference and Portuguese translation.

runs.text: ſaudades da peßoa que gostaua diſto, o que ſe

lines.note: The Portuguese explains longing for the person who used to enjoy this. The beta-shaped double-s sort in peßoa is preserved as in the baseline, without conflating it with two independently visible long-s types.
The translation says that the tears do not run out. The scan retains the unusual printed eſgosta; it is not silently corrected to modern esgota merely because the latter is expected semantically.
Kyouman is equated with manki and glossed as pride or arrogance. The tilde in arrogãcia abbreviates its nasal consonant.
Haughtiness completes the list of senses. Altiueza retains the printed historical u rather than modern v.
Oshie no ajiwai is the taste or savour of a teaching, matching gosto da ley. The Portuguese continues to doctrine below rather than introducing the modern general sense of interest.

Doutrina completes the object of the taste metaphor. The final upright S marks written usage and is not part of the italic translation. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
The example means writing down someone's name. The complete upright headword and repeated example correct OCR O eômiǒ and Q eômiǒ; the Portuguese begins Eſcre-, not Eſtre-.
Completes escrever o nome dalguem, to write someone's name. The initial u continues the historical spelling of the divided Portuguese verb.
Warui yatsuko explains a bad servant or slave. The initial word is Qeônu, not the OCR's separated Q cônu.

runs.text: peruerſo, & maluado. Aliquando he o meſmo

lines.note: The servant is described as perverse and wicked. Aliquando introduces an occasional equivalence to Qeôto on the following row; the worn n is retained from the aligned reading.
Qeôto completes the comparison within the Portuguese explanation and is followed by 'dissolute and idle men'. Its initial Q corrects OCR ǒ; the whole Japanese cross-reference remains upright.

runs.text: Conſelho, ou auiſo em couſas de vir-

lines.note: Kyouke denotes counsel or instruction concerning virtue or salvation. Vir- begins virtude, not a separate abbreviated label.
The example begins hito ni kyouke wo nasu, giving someone this kind of counsel. Na- continues the verb on the next row.
Su completes nasu; suru is given as an alternative. The Portuguese says to give advice on this subject, with materia divided after ma-.
Teria completes materia and closes the religious-counsel entry. Its short length does not change its status as body text.
Kyoukyou is paraphrased by repeated osore, fear or deference. Pa is entirely italic and begins palaura below; no terminal hyphen is visible.

runs.text: laura que ſe eſcreue no cabo das cartas. Como

lines.note: Palaura completes the description of a word written at the end of letters. The following comparison explains its deferential pragmatic force.

runs.text: quem diz, indigno de vos eſcreuer, &c. S.

lines.note: The formula is explained as expressing unworthiness to write to the addressee. Upright S labels written usage, consistent with its epistolary function. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Osore tsutsushimu describes fear and reverent restraint. The scan supports Voſore, not OCR Voſote, and the complete Qeôqin without an inserted space.
Reverence completes the gloss alongside fear. The final upright S is the written-language label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

The gloss concerns conjugal union, with majiwari as the Japanese explanation. The short second form is retained as printed uǒ after enlarged inspection; its unusual spelling is not expanded into an inferred modern verb.
The union is specifically that of husband and wife. Fuufu no kyouquai begins the example; the long-u mark is worn but the baseline caron reading is retained.
Quai completes the divided example noun. S is the upright written-usage label, not an italic Portuguese continuation. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Kyouri denotes one's native place; the example means leaving it. The repeated Japanese word is contiguous, correcting the OCR's internal space, and the Portuguese verb starts A-.
Completes apartarse longe de sua patria: going far away from one's homeland. This is the translation of saru, not another headword.

Kangae hakaru explains considering and estimating, matching conjecture or calculation. A faint but visible caron survives over the final o in Qeôriǒ; that mark is less clear than the first circumflex and remains a nonblocking reading caveat.

runs.text: conta que ſe faz ſobre algũa couſa.

lines.note: Completes a calculation or estimate made about something. Algũa retains its u-carried abbreviation tilde.
Ashiki shukke explains an ill-behaved religious practitioner. The scan supports the complete Qeôſô and its tall long-s type, rather than OCR Q côſô.

The alternative description is a bad bonze. The final upright S marks written usage; the Portuguese designation Bonzo remains italic. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Kyousoku is described as a small bench serving as a support. This material object is distinct from the preceding religious-person entry.
De encosto completes the function as a support or rest. The lower-right Qeôtai is a separate catchword, not a continuation of this definition.
